notes.meaning: Joseph respectfully reports his family's arrival to Pharaoh before settling them anywhere. Even though Pharaoh had already invited them, Joseph honors the king's authority and seeks royal approval for their stay in Goshen. Showing proper respect to those in authority honors God.

Joseph chooses five of his brothers to introduce them directly to the king. Presenting only a few brothers kept the royal meeting orderly while giving Pharaoh a clear impression of the whole family. Joseph took great care to present his family honorably before the ruler of Egypt.

Pharaoh asks the brothers about their line of work, just as Joseph had expected. The brothers answer honestly that they and their ancestors have always been shepherds. Being truthful about our everyday work pleases God and keeps us humble.

The brothers explain that the severe famine in Canaan has dried up every pasture, leaving no food for their flocks. They make it clear that they have come only to stay for a short time, not to take over Egyptian land permanently. By speaking plainly, they ask for permission to live in the green pastures of Goshen.

Pharaoh welcomes Joseph's family and tells him to give them the very best pastureland in Egypt, the region of Goshen. He also invites Joseph to place any skilled, capable brothers in charge of the royal livestock. God moved Pharaoh's heart to provide generously for the entire family of Israel.

Joseph brings his aged father Jacob in to meet Pharaoh, and Jacob begins the meeting by blessing the king. Although Pharaoh was a mighty ruler, Jacob spoke as God's servant and pronounced God's favor over him. This encounter shows that true spiritual authority comes from God rather than earthly power.

Pharaoh is struck by the old man's appearance and asks Jacob how old he is. People in Egypt rarely lived to such an advanced age, so Jacob's appearance filled the royal court with wonder. A long life lived in faithfulness to God deserves deep honor and respect.

Jacob replies that his life has lasted 130 years and describes his days as a pilgrimage, meaning he lived as a wanderer whose true home was elsewhere. He calls his years few and hard because he had suffered many heartaches, and he had not lived as long as Abraham or Isaac. Believers are reminded that this earthly life is only a short journey on the way to our true home with God.

Jacob blesses Pharaoh once more before leaving the royal presence. He offered a sincere prayer of thanks for the king's kindness to his family. Believers are called to show gratitude and ask God's blessing on leaders who act with generosity.

Joseph obeys Pharaoh's command and settles his father and brothers in the district of Rameses, which was part of Goshen. This was the most fertile part of Egypt, offering green grass and plenty of space for their flocks. God kept His promise to care for His people by placing them in the finest part of the country.

Joseph provides steady food for his father, brothers, and all their households according to the size of each family. He made sure that everyone was nourished, from the oldest adult down to the youngest child. In his tender care, Joseph shows how God faithfully feeds and shelters His people in times of trouble.

The famine grew so harsh that all grain supplies ran out across Egypt and Canaan, leaving the people weak from hunger. Even the most fertile farming areas could produce nothing without rain and the overflow of the Nile. When earthly resources fail, people are forced to see how completely they depend on God for daily bread.

Joseph sold stored grain to the people of Egypt and Canaan until he had gathered all the available money. Instead of keeping any of this vast fortune for himself, he brought every coin into Pharaoh's royal treasury. True godly character means managing wealth with complete honesty and without selfish greed.

When all the money was gone, the Egyptians came to Joseph begging for food so they would not starve to death. Silver and gold could no longer buy life once the money had run out. In their desperate need, they cast themselves entirely upon Joseph's mercy.

Joseph told the people to bring their livestock in trade for food since their money was spent. The people brought their horses, donkeys, sheep, and cattle, and Joseph gave them enough grain to sustain them through that year. This wise plan kept the people fed while also saving the animals from dying of thirst and hunger.

The next year, the Egyptians returned and confessed that they had nothing left to give except their own bodies and their fields. They pleaded with Joseph to buy them and their land in exchange for grain, offering to become Pharaoh's servants, and asked for seed so the land would not turn into a desert. They willingly surrendered their property and freedom so that their families might survive.

Joseph purchased all the farmland in Egypt for Pharaoh because the extreme famine forced every citizen to sell. The king became the legal owner of all the fields in the land. Joseph fulfilled his official duties faithfully and without using violence or unfair pressure.

Joseph relocated the farming families into cities across Egypt where the food storehouses were kept. Bringing the scattered population near the grain supplies made it easier to feed everyone and keep them alive during the crisis. This major change helped the people see that their very survival came through the king's storehouses.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some ancient translations and modern scholars read the verse as saying Joseph made the Egyptians slaves or servants, rather than moving them into the cities.

notes.meaning: Joseph did not buy the land belonging to the Egyptian priests because Pharaoh provided them with regular food rations. Since the crown fed them during the famine, the priests never had to sell their ancestral property. Even a pagan ruler recognized an obligation to support the ministers of religion.

Joseph provided the people with seed to plant their fields and set a permanent tax of one-fifth of the crop for Pharaoh. The people were allowed to keep four-fifths for their own food, their families, and future planting. Instead of treating them like miserable slaves, Joseph gave them reasonable terms to rebuild their lives and keep working.

The people responded with deep gratitude, declaring that Joseph had saved their lives, and gladly agreed to be Pharaoh's servants. They understood that his policies were fair and had rescued them from certain death. When someone saves us from ruin, serving them becomes a willing and joyful choice.

Joseph turned this agreement into a permanent law throughout Egypt, requiring that one-fifth of all crops belong to the crown, while the priests' land remained exempt. This system stood as the national economic law for many generations. It demonstrated Joseph's wisdom in protecting the king's rights while ensuring that the common people could thrive.

The people of Israel settled peacefully in Goshen, acquired property, and multiplied greatly in number. While the Egyptians had to sell their goods and land to survive, God's covenant family grew and prospered under divine care. This growth began the fulfillment of God's promise to turn Jacob's household into a mighty nation.

Jacob lived in Egypt for seventeen years, bringing his whole lifespan to 147 years. Jacob had raised Joseph for his first seventeen years, and now Joseph was able to support his elderly father for the last seventeen years of his life. God in His kindness gave Jacob a quiet and comforted old age after many years of pain.

As Jacob felt his death drawing near, he called Joseph and asked him to place his hand under his thigh to make a sacred oath. He pleaded with Joseph not to bury him in Egypt, but to carry his body back to Canaan to rest with Abraham and Isaac. Jacob made this request in faith, knowing Canaan was the promised land and a picture of the eternal rest God gives His people.

Jacob insisted that Joseph swear an oath, and when Joseph did, Jacob bowed in worship at the head of his bed. Though old and weak, the patriarch used what strength he had left to thank God for answering his final request. God's people can face death in peace, resting on His promises and offering grateful praise.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Greek versions and the New Testament in Hebrews 11:21 state that Jacob leaned on the top of his staff to worship, which in Hebrew uses the same consonants as the word for bed.
